questions.stem: What news sets the novel's plot in motion?
options: Lady Catherine has invited the Bennet girls to stay at Rosings
A rich single man, Mr Bingley, has rented nearby Netherfield Park
Mr Bennet has lost his fortune and must sell Longbourn to Mr Darcy
A regiment of soldiers has arrived to stay in Longbourn House
questions.explanation: Mrs Bennet sees Bingley, with 'four or five thousand a year', as a husband for one of her daughters. The opening makes marriage and money the novel's subject.

questions.stem: What does Darcy do at the Meryton assembly that offends Elizabeth?
options: He refuses to dance with her, saying she is not handsome enough to tempt him
He dances with her twice but criticises her family loudly to Mr Bingley
He asks her to dance and then leaves the room before the music begins
He tells her sister Jane that Elizabeth is too poor to marry a gentleman
questions.explanation: Elizabeth overhears Darcy's insult. Her first impression of him as proud and rude shapes how she judges everything he does afterwards.

questions.stem: Why does Jane end up staying several days at Netherfield?
options: Her sisters leave her behind after a ball, and she has no way home
Her mother sends her on horseback in the rain, and she falls ill there
Her carriage breaks down on the road, and the Bingleys invite her in
Her father sends her to fetch a letter, and Mr Bingley asks her to stay
questions.explanation: Mrs Bennet hopes rain will force Jane to stay. Jane catches cold, and Elizabeth walks three miles through the mud to nurse her, which shocks the Bingley sisters.

questions.stem: What story does Wickham tell Elizabeth about Darcy?
options: That Darcy denied him the church living Darcy's father meant him to have
That Darcy stole his inheritance and forced him to join the militia
That Darcy fought a duel with him over a woman in London years ago
That Darcy spread lies that cost Wickham a place at Cambridge
questions.explanation: Elizabeth believes Wickham at once because it fits her dislike of Darcy. His charm and her prejudice blind her to the strangeness of a near-stranger sharing such a story.

questions.stem: What happens after Elizabeth refuses Mr Collins's proposal?
options: Within days he proposes to Charlotte Lucas, who accepts him
He leaves Longbourn in anger and returns at once to Hunsford
He proposes to Jane instead, who refuses him even more firmly
He asks Lady Catherine to persuade Elizabeth to change her mind
questions.explanation: Collins quickly transfers his proposal to Charlotte. Elizabeth is shocked that her sensible friend would marry such a foolish man for security.

questions.stem: Where does Darcy first propose to Elizabeth?
options: At the Hunsford parsonage in Kent, while she is visiting Charlotte
At Pemberley, while she is touring Derbyshire with Mr and Mrs Gardiner
At the Netherfield ball, while they are dancing together
At Longbourn, after he returns with Bingley in the autumn
questions.explanation: Darcy calls while Elizabeth is alone at the parsonage near Rosings. The proposal turns into a bitter argument about Jane and Wickham.

questions.stem: What does Darcy's letter after the first proposal reveal?
options: Bingley was already engaged to Darcy's sister Georgiana
Lady Catherine had forced Darcy to propose against his will
Wickham tried to elope with Darcy's young sister for her fortune
Wickham is Darcy's half-brother and the rightful heir to the Pemberley estate
questions.explanation: Darcy explains that Wickham gave up the church living for money, then tried to elope with Georgiana when she was fifteen. He also explains why he separated Bingley from Jane.

questions.stem: How does Darcy behave when Elizabeth unexpectedly meets him at Pemberley?
options: He is cold and distant, and avoids her for the rest of her visit
He is angry, and asks the housekeeper to show the visitors out
He is embarrassed, and leaves at once for his house in London
He is courteous and warm, even to her aunt and uncle Gardiner
questions.explanation: Darcy invites Mr Gardiner to fish and asks to introduce his sister. His changed manners, and his housekeeper's praise, show Elizabeth a different man.

questions.stem: What news reaches Elizabeth at Lambton, near Pemberley?
options: Mr Bennet has died suddenly at home
Kitty has run away with an officer
Lydia has run away with Wickham
Jane has become engaged to Bingley
questions.explanation: Jane's letters report that Lydia has eloped from Brighton with Wickham, who seems to have no plan to marry her. The scandal threatens the whole family.

questions.stem: How does Elizabeth learn of Darcy's part in Lydia's marriage?
options: Wickham boasts about it at dinner to embarrass Darcy in front of her
Lydia lets slip that Darcy was at her wedding, and Mrs Gardiner explains
Darcy tells her himself when he calls at Longbourn with Mr Bingley
Lady Catherine accuses her of it when she visits Longbourn in anger
questions.explanation: Darcy found the couple, paid Wickham's debts and arranged the marriage, and asked for secrecy. Mrs Gardiner's letter tells Elizabeth the truth.

questions.stem: Why does Lady Catherine de Bourgh come to Longbourn near the end?
options: To invite Elizabeth to live at Rosings as her companion
To tell the Bennets that Mr Collins has now inherited Longbourn House
To beg Elizabeth to persuade Jane to break off with Bingley
To make Elizabeth promise never to accept an offer from Darcy
questions.explanation: Lady Catherine has heard a rumour of an engagement. Elizabeth refuses to promise anything, and when Darcy hears of it, he dares to hope and proposes again.

questions.stem: How do Darcy's two proposals work as a structural pair?
options: The first is overheard by Lady Catherine, the second by Mr Bennet
The first shows both characters' pride and prejudice, the second their growth
The first is made in a letter, the second in person in front of her whole family
The first is accepted and then broken off, the second ends in a quarrel
questions.explanation: At Hunsford Darcy is insulting and Elizabeth unfair. The second proposal shows both humbled and wiser, so the novel's shape traces their change.

questions.stem: Mr Bennet is best described as:
options: witty and detached, but neglectful of his duty as a father
stern and strict, but devoted to all five of his young daughters
anxious and nervous, but determined to marry off his girls
foolish and pompous, but well-meaning towards his family
questions.explanation: Mr Bennet enjoys mocking his wife and younger daughters but does nothing to correct them. His failure to control Lydia leads to the elopement.

questions.stem: What is described as 'the business of her life' for Mrs Bennet?
options: Getting her daughters married
Managing the Longbourn estate
Visiting the poor of the parish
Keeping her husband in good health
questions.explanation: The narrator adds that 'its solace was visiting and news'. Mrs Bennet is comic, but her anxiety has a real cause: the entail will leave her daughters homeless.

questions.stem: Mr Collins is best described as:
options: a clever, cynical lawyer who manages the Bennet estate
a dashing army officer who charms the younger sisters
a pompous, flattering clergyman who worships Lady Catherine
a shy, gentle clergyman who loves Elizabeth from afar
questions.explanation: Austen calls him 'not a sensible man'. His heavy compliments and endless praise of his patroness make him one of her great comic creations.

questions.stem: Why does Charlotte Lucas accept Mr Collins?
options: Her father has lost his fortune and forces her to marry the first man
She wants to live near Lady Catherine, whom she greatly admires
He offers her a home and security, which she values more than love
She has secretly loved him since they first met at the Lucas house
questions.explanation: Charlotte is twenty-seven, plain and without fortune. She tells Elizabeth 'I ask only a comfortable home', and the novel treats her choice with sympathy as well as regret.

questions.stem: George Wickham is best described as:
options: dull and awkward, but loyal and well-meaning
proud and reserved, but generous in secret
silly and noisy, but harmless to others
charming and handsome, but dishonest and in debt
questions.explanation: Wickham's easy manners win everyone over. His lies about Darcy and his elopement with Lydia show that appearances can deceive.

questions.stem: Darcy says late in the novel, 'I have been a selfish being all my life, in practice, though not in principle.' What change does this show?
options: He blames his parents for spoiling him and refuses to change his ways
He admits that he never loved Elizabeth and proposed only from duty
He recognises that his pride hurt others and accepts Elizabeth's criticism
He still believes his pride was justified but agrees to hide it from others
questions.explanation: Darcy has taken Elizabeth's reproof to heart. Like her, he has had to learn to know himself, so both lovers change.

questions.stem: What does the entail on Longbourn mean for the Bennets?
options: The estate must pass to a male heir, Mr Collins, not to the daughters
The estate must be sold when Mr Bennet dies and the money shared
The estate must go to whichever daughter marries first
The estate must be given to the Church when the family dies out
questions.explanation: Because Mr Bennet has no son, Longbourn will go to his cousin Collins. His wife and daughters face losing their home, which makes marriage urgent.

questions.stem: The novel was first drafted under the title First Impressions. Why does that title suit it?
options: Elizabeth and Darcy both misjudge each other at first and must learn better
The story covers only the first few days after the Bennets meet Bingley
Bingley's first impression of Jane proves to be mistaken
The novel shows that trusting one's instincts on a first meeting is usually wise
questions.explanation: Elizabeth's first view of Darcy and her quick trust in Wickham are both wrong. The novel is about the danger of judging too fast.

questions.stem: Why was marriage so important for women of Elizabeth's class in Austen's time?
options: Women gained the right to vote once they were married
Women could rarely inherit or earn a living, so marriage decided their future
Women who married could keep and manage their own inheritance, unlike single women
Women were required by law to marry a man chosen by their father
questions.explanation: A gentleman's daughter could not take up a profession, and estates often passed to male heirs. A good marriage meant a home and security.

questions.stem: Why does Lydia's elopement threaten all the Bennet sisters, not just Lydia?
options: Wickham could now claim a share of the Bennet estate through his marriage to Lydia
Lydia had taken the family's money, leaving the others without dowries
Mr Collins could claim Longbourn at once if any daughter eloped
A sister's disgrace damaged the whole family's reputation and marriage hopes
questions.explanation: Mr Collins writes that Lydia's fall will harm her sisters' prospects. Darcy's secret help saves the family's respectability, and Elizabeth's chances too.

questions.stem: Elizabeth tells Lady Catherine, 'He is a gentleman; I am a gentleman's daughter; so far we are equal.' What is she arguing?
options: That her birth makes her a fit wife for Darcy, whatever her connections
That she and Darcy have the same income and are equally rich
That rank matters less than love in choosing a husband
That Darcy has lowered himself by courting a woman so far beneath his rank
questions.explanation: Lady Catherine objects to Elizabeth's family and her relations in trade. Elizabeth answers that, by rank, she and Darcy are equals.

questions.stem: Which idea is most central to Pride and Prejudice?
options: The rewards of obeying one's parents in choosing a husband
The superiority of country life to life in London society
The triumph of romantic passion over social convention
The danger of hasty judgements and the need to know oneself
questions.explanation: Both Elizabeth and Darcy misjudge each other and must face their own faults. Elizabeth's 'Till this moment, I never knew myself' marks this turning point.

questions.stem: Which statement best describes the title's two qualities?
options: Pride belongs to the Bingleys and prejudice to Lady Catherine
Pride is presented as a virtue, and prejudice as the real fault
Darcy and Elizabeth each show both pride and prejudice in different ways
Darcy is the novel's figure of pride, and Elizabeth its figure of prejudice
questions.explanation: Darcy's pride leads to his prejudice against her family; Elizabeth's wounded pride leads to her prejudice against him. The neat pairing breaks down on a close reading.

questions.stem: The novel presents several marriages. What do they show together?
options: Marriages based on passion, like Lydia's, are the novel's ideal
Marriages built on money or passion alone fail; respect and affection last
Marriages made for security, like Charlotte's, prove the happiest in the novel
Marriages in the country are happier than marriages in the town
questions.explanation: The Bennets' mismatch, Lydia's reckless match and Charlotte's practical one contrast with Elizabeth and Darcy, who marry with knowledge and esteem.

questions.stem: What is ironic about the opening sentence, 'It is a truth universally acknowledged, that a single man in possession of a good fortune must be in want of a wife'?
options: In fact Mrs Bennet says it to persuade her husband to call on Mr Bingley
In fact it is families with daughters who want single men with fortunes
In fact it is a sincere statement of the narrator's own view
In fact most men in the novel marry for money, not love
questions.explanation: The grand 'truth' is really the wish of mothers like Mrs Bennet. Austen's irony announces the novel's satirical view of marriage and money.

questions.stem: How is the story mostly narrated?
options: In the third person, through Mrs Bennet's eyes and opinions
In the third person, often through Elizabeth's thoughts, with ironic comment
In the first person, by Elizabeth writing to her sister Jane in London
In the first person, by Darcy looking back on how he won Elizabeth
questions.explanation: Austen uses free indirect discourse to let us share Elizabeth's view, including her mistakes. We misjudge Darcy with her until the letter.

questions.stem: Why is Darcy's letter after the first proposal so important to the novel's structure?
options: It is the climax, in which Darcy proposes for the second and final time
It is the resolution, in which Elizabeth finally accepts Darcy's second proposal
It is the crisis, in which Lydia's elopement is first revealed
It is the turning point that forces Elizabeth to re-read everything she believed
questions.explanation: Elizabeth reads and re-reads the letter, and her view of Wickham and Darcy changes. A letter lets Darcy explain himself without interruption.

questions.stem: How does Austen use Pemberley when Elizabeth first sees it?
options: Its small, plain house suggests Darcy is poorer than people think
Its natural, tasteful grounds suggest Darcy's true character
Its grand, showy rooms suggest Darcy's love of wealth and display
Its ruined, neglected gardens suggest Darcy's careless pride
questions.explanation: Elizabeth sees grounds where natural beauty is not spoilt by 'awkward taste', and rooms 'neither gaudy nor uselessly fine'. The setting hints that Darcy's real nature is better than his manners suggested.

questions.stem: Darcy begins his first proposal: 'In vain have I struggled. It will not do. My feelings will not be repressed.' What does this opening reveal?
options: He has fought against loving her, which makes the proposal insulting
He has loved her from the start and is sure that she loves him in return
He is proposing out of duty to his family, not from real feeling
He is nervous because he expects Elizabeth to accept him at once
questions.explanation: Darcy goes on to dwell on her inferior connections. He means it as a compliment to the strength of his love, but Elizabeth hears his pride.

questions.stem: Who says 'had you behaved in a more gentlemanlike manner'?
options: Lady Catherine, scolding Elizabeth at Longbourn
Jane, defending Bingley against her mother
Mr Bennet, reproaching Wickham after the wedding
Elizabeth, refusing Darcy's first proposal
questions.explanation: The words wound Darcy, who repeats them during the second proposal. They show how the criticism helped change him.

questions.stem: Elizabeth thinks, 'Till this moment, I never knew myself.' When does she think it?
options: After touring Pemberley and realising how rich Darcy is
After hearing that Lydia has eloped and fearing for her family
After refusing Mr Collins and arguing with her mother
After reading Darcy's letter and seeing how she misjudged him and Wickham
questions.explanation: Elizabeth realises she has been 'blind, partial, prejudiced'. Admitting her own fault is the start of her change.

questions.stem: Charlotte tells Elizabeth, 'I am not romantic, you know.' What does she mean?
options: She does not enjoy novels and prefers to read books of sermons instead
She thinks Jane should show Bingley more affection than she feels
She wants Elizabeth to accept Mr Collins after all
She is marrying Mr Collins for a comfortable home, not for love
questions.explanation: Charlotte goes on: 'I ask only a comfortable home'. Her honesty shows the narrow choices facing women without money.

questions.stem: Mr Bennet asks, 'For what do we live, but to make sport for our neighbours, and laugh at them in our turn?' What does this reveal about him?
options: His ironic detachment, which helps him avoid acting seriously as a father
His deep shame, which makes him decide to reform his whole household
His kindness, which makes him forgive his neighbours their gossip
His anger, which makes him threaten to leave Longbourn for London
questions.explanation: Even near the end Mr Bennet treats life as a comedy. His wit is attractive, but his detachment allowed Lydia's disgrace.

questions.stem: Lady Catherine cries, 'Are the shades of Pemberley to be thus polluted?' What does it show?
options: Her snobbery about Elizabeth's family, linked now to Wickham
Her fear that the Pemberley estate will be ruined by floods
Her anger that Darcy has kept his engagement a secret from her
Her worry that Elizabeth will waste Darcy's fortune
questions.explanation: Lady Catherine is horrified that the son of Pemberley's steward could become Darcy's brother-in-law. Her pride in rank is the comic extreme of Darcy's own.

questions.stem: Mr Bennet tells Elizabeth, 'From this day you must be a stranger to one of your parents.' What is the situation?
options: Her mother insists she marry Mr Collins, and her father backs her refusal
Her father insists she marry Darcy, and her mother forbids the match
Her parents are separating, and she must choose which one she will live with
Her father is sending her to live with Lady Catherine at Rosings
questions.explanation: Mrs Bennet will never see her again if she refuses Collins; Mr Bennet will never see her again if she accepts. It is comic, and it shows the father valuing her judgement.

questions.stem: For the question 'How does Austen explore the dangers of first impressions in Pride and Prejudice?', which is the strongest topic sentence?
options: Pride and Prejudice is a novel by Jane Austen that was first published in 1813
This essay will explore how Austen shows the idea of first impressions in Pride and Prejudice
Elizabeth Bennet meets Mr Darcy at the Meryton assembly in the first chapters
Austen shows that Elizabeth's quick judgement of Darcy blinds her to Wickham's lies
questions.explanation: A strong topic sentence names the author, makes a claim that answers the question and points to evidence. The others give facts, announce or retell.

questions.stem: A student writes: 'Mrs Bennet talks a lot about her nerves and wants her daughters to marry.' How could this be turned into analysis?
options: Describe what Mrs Bennet wears to the Netherfield ball in more detail
Explain how her comic anxiety reflects the real threat the entail poses to her family
Add the names of all five daughters and the order in which they were born
List more of the things Mrs Bennet complains about during the novel
questions.explanation: Analysis explains what the evidence shows. Linking her comedy to the entail connects a character detail to the novel's ideas about money and women.
